input.message:
Additional angle to evaluate, likely the biggest single win. Fold it into your report; don't restart what you already have.

Hypothesis: the wasm build can drop the segment implementations entirely, not just their detection code.

Facts I've established here, so you don't need to re-derive them:

1. `src/config/segment_types.go:394` is `var Segments = map[SegmentType]func() SegmentWriter{...}` with 118 entries, each closing over a concrete `segments.X{}`. A package-level map initialised with all 118 constructors is reachable from any config parse, so every segment type and its whole interface method set survives dead-code elimination. This is almost certainly why the cloud SDKs / HTTP clients are linked. Verify that claim against your actual size measurements.

2. Segment detection DOES still execute in the browser today. `src/config/segment.go:546` documents that nothing is gated on `runtime.Flags.DataOnly` deliberately - the flag makes the environment refuse probes, but `writer.Enabled()` still runs. So the studio pays for that code both in bytes and in execution.

3. The reason the concrete structs are needed at all is that recorded data is restored ONTO the writer struct, and templates then read fields and call methods on it.

The hypothesis: point 3 is avoidable. I verified that Go's text/template resolves a name against a MAP KEY when the value is a map, so `{{ .Working.String }}` renders identically from `map[string]any{"Working": map[string]any{"String": "+2 ~1"}}` as it does from a real `segments.GitStatus` with a `String()` method. A recorded method *result* is indistinguishable to the template from a live method call. Proven with a standalone program.

So a wasm build could in principle carry no `src/segments` at all, feeding the engine plain maps.

What I need you to assess and measure:

a) How much of the 28MB is actually attributable to `src/segments` and its transitive deps? Measure it - e.g. build a variant with a `js && wasm`-tagged `Segments` map containing zero (or a handful of) entries and report raw/gzip/brotli. That variant does not need to render correctly; it is a size probe. This is the number that decides whether any of this is worth doing.

b) What breaks, concretely:
   - 65 of the 124 bundled themes call `.Working.String` / `.Staging.String` / `.State.String`. These are recordable as map keys per the above, but confirm the recorder (`src/cli/config_export_data.go`) currently captures struct fields via json tags and would need to also capture computed method results. Scope that change.
   - 98 segments define a default `Template() string` in Go (`grep -rl "func (.*) Template() string" src/segments/*.go`). A config that omits `template` relies on these. Dropping the packages loses them. Assess extracting them into a generated `map[SegmentType]string` table that the wasm build embeds - it is just strings, so it should be cheap. Measure the table's size.
   - 55 exported zero-arg methods exist across segment types that a user template could call. In the studio a user can write an arbitrary config, so anything not pre-recorded would render empty. Judge how bad that is and whether a fallback is needed.
   - The json-tag-to-template-name mapping (docs mention wakatime storing `.CumulativeTotal` as `cumulative_total`) also lives with the structs.

c) Whether a smaller intermediate step gets most of the win for much less risk - e.g. keeping the structs but excluding only the heaviest transitive deps (cloud SDKs) behind build tags.

Report a) first and lead with it. If a) turns out to be small, say so plainly and the rest is moot.

content.thinking:
I'm trying to understand why the build regenerated when it shouldn't have. The binary was built earlier, and then the artifacts got regenerated around 13:30 when I ran the theme build. Now I'm checking whether the staleness calculation is comparing the binary's modification time against the artifacts correctly, but I'm getting confused about when the binary was actually last rebuilt.

Actually, I think I've got it now — the `go build` command I ran to measure performance rewrote the binary's mtime, which made it newer than the artifacts that were generated earlier. So the staleness check is working correctly; my test sequence just created that condition. The real issue is that Go always rewrites the binary on every build, even if nothing changed, which means any manual `go build` will invalidate the artifacts. But that's actually the right behavior — if someone rebuilds the binary, the rendered output might differ, so regenerating artifacts makes sense.

Let me verify there's no infinite loop by running the ensure-artifacts command twice in a row and checking that the second run is truly a no-op.

input.command:
Set-Location D:\oh-my-posh\website; Remove-Item Env:\OMP_BIN -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
node scripts/ensure-artifacts.mjs *> $null
"--- run 2 (should be silent no-op) ---"
$t=Measure-Command { node scripts/ensure-artifacts.mjs 2>&1 | Tee-Object -Variable o }
"output lines: $($o.Count)   took $([math]::Round($t.TotalSeconds,1))s"

Your instinct is right, and I proved the load-bearing part: Go's `text/template` resolves a name against a **map key** when the value is a map, so `{{ .Working.String }}` renders `+2 ~1` from `map[string]any{"String": "+2 ~1"}` exactly as it does from a real `segments.GitStatus` method. To a template, a recorded method *result* is indistinguishable from a live method call. So the writer structs aren't fundamentally required — plain maps would drive the engine identically.

Three things still tie the wasm build to `src/segments`, all of them solvable rather than fundamental:

- **The recorder captures fields, not method results.** `config export data` writes struct fields via json tags. 65 of the 124 bundled themes call `.Working.String`, `.Staging.String` or `.State.String`, so those results would have to be recorded as ordinary keys.
- **98 segments define a default `Template()` in Go.** A config that omits `template` depends on them. They're just string constants, so a generated `map[SegmentType]string` table would carry them for almost nothing.
- **55 exported zero-arg methods** exist across segment types. The studio takes arbitrary configs, so anything a user calls that wasn't pre-recorded renders empty. That's the real fidelity question, and it's a judgement call rather than a blocker.

I've handed all of this to Fable with the framing that (a) — how many of the 28 MB `src/segments` and its transitive deps actually account for — gets measured first, because if that number is small the rest is moot. It should probe it with a `js && wasm`-tagged registry containing zero entries; that variant doesn't need to render, it just needs to weigh.

**Meanwhile, everything else landed and verified:**

The rprompt shows at 120 columns — the hero now ends ` in zsh at 09:41:00`. `Engine.RPromptBreathingRoom` overrides the interactive 30, and only `render.Config` sets it. Interactive shells are untouched, the goldens all pass, and **zero of the 124 gallery themes changed** — none sat in the 20–29 cell window.

content.text:
No, but removing it wouldn't buy anything in production — and that's the important part.

`DumpRequestOut` is guarded by `if term.CmdFlags.Debug` at [terminal.go:490](src/runtime/terminal.go:490), so it only *runs* with `--debug`. It's linked unconditionally either way. It builds a `Transport` internally because its whole purpose is to show the request as it goes on the wire, including the headers the transport adds (`Host`, `User-Agent`, `Accept-Encoding`).

But the production CLI already constructs a real `Transport` at [http.go:17](src/runtime/http/http.go:17) — `defaultTransport`, with proxy support and TLS handshake timeouts — because segments genuinely make HTTPS calls. The TLS stack is required there regardless. So dropping `DumpRequestOut` from the production build saves approximately nothing: the same code stays reachable through the client that actually does the work.

Where it matters is precisely the wasm build. There, `http.go`'s transport would be stubbed out anyway — and `DumpRequestOut` would silently keep the entire TLS stack alive despite that, defeating the stub. That's what makes it the non-obvious find: it's a *second*, hidden construction site, and both have to go for the ~7 MB to drop.

Two ways to handle it, depending on how much you care about `--debug` fidelity:

- **`httputil.DumpRequest` instead of `DumpRequestOut`.** Same signature, no `Transport`. You lose the transport-added headers, keeping method, URL, your own headers and the body — which is what actually matters when debugging a segment against an API. It's also body-safe, restoring the reader after reading it.
- **Log the fields directly** and drop `httputil` entirely. More code, no dependency at all.

Either is a one-line-ish change to the real source, which is cleaner than carrying a `js && wasm` stub for it. Worth doing on its own merits even before the wasm question is settled — a debug-only dump reaching for the network stack is a surprising coupling.

I'd hold off until Fable's compressed numbers land, though. If `nohttp` turns out not to compress well, the whole line of work may not be worth the stub maintenance, and this change would be solving a problem nobody has.

content.text:
Direct answer: **the library earns its place, the LUT doesn't.**

What we use it for is narrow — `RuneWidth` at four call sites in `writer.go`, classifying each rune as 0, 1 or 2 cells. That feeds prompt length (which drives rprompt placement, right-block padding and fill) and `countVisibleCells` for gradient interpolation. Nothing else.

But the width data isn't something to hand-roll. I built a candidate from stdlib `unicode` categories plus `x/text/width` — both already linked, zero init cost — and diffed it against runewidth across all 1,114,112 runes: **2,648 disagreements**, including 360 runes where runewidth says 2 and the candidate says 1. Those are emoji, which people absolutely put in prompt configs, and each one silently misaligns the prompt by a cell. Reimplementing means owning Unicode width tables, which is precisely what the library is for.

The LUT is a different matter:

| | |
|---|---|
| LUT path (as shipped) | **751 ns** per 80-rune prompt |
| no-LUT path | **703 ns** per prompt |
| init cost of building the LUT | **26 ms**, every process |

It saves ~48 ns per render and is within noise of being *slower*. Break-even is around half a million renders in one process. oh-my-posh does one or two, then exits.

And it can't be configured away. `Condition.RuneWidth` only *consults* the LUT when `StrictEmojiNeutral` is set, but `init()` *builds* it unconditionally — so any binary linking the package pays 26 ms whether it touches the LUT or not. Downgrading isn't an option either: v0.0.24 has no LUT and 0 ms init, but its width data is wrong for 1,239 runes, mostly Hebrew and Arabic combining marks that must be zero-width.

The telling detail is that upstream already has an opt-in LUT — `Condition.CreateLUT()`, documented as "will create an in-memory lookup table of 557056 bytes for faster operation". Having that *and* an eager one in `init` looks like an oversight rather than a design. A `sync.Once` around `initStrictWidthLUT`, or gating it behind the same opt-in, would fix it for every short-lived Go program, not just ours.

Two ways to get it today, and I'd want your call before doing either: a `replace` directive onto a patched fork, or an upstream issue/PR and we wait. Vendoring a dependency isn't a decision I should make on my own.

Worth being clear about the scope, though — this stopped being a wasm question two measurements ago. It's ~26 ms on **every prompt render of the real CLI**, roughly 10% of a 240 ms render, and per your pwsh notes an Enter spawns two processes, so ~50 ms per keypress.

Where the rest landed:

- **nohttp: done and measured.** −11.1% raw, −10.2% brotli, matching the probe. `runtime/http` splits into tagged default/js clients, the debug dump moves behind `runtime/httpdump{,_js}.go`, and `DumpRequestOut` becomes `DumpRequest` — which is worth having regardless, since a debug-only dump shouldn't reach for the network stack.
- **dsc: tried, reverted.** I moved cobra into a `dsc/cmd` subpackage expecting the clean no-build-tags win. It gained **−1,366 bytes**, i.e. noise — cobra wasn't the cost. The real 37 KB is jsonschema and yaml/v4 in `resource.go`, which only a tagged duplicate of a 134-line file would remove. Poor trade for 0.9%, so I left it alone.
- **Registry redesign: not started.** It's the biggest win but it's the maps-fed-engine work, gated on segment detection no longer running in-browser. That's a feature, not a tweak, and I'd want to scope it separately.

Both done, plus a latent bug the work exposed.

**`nohttp` — shipped and verified.** `runtime/http` splits into tagged default/js clients, the debug dump moves behind `runtime/httpdump{,_js}.go`, and `DumpRequestOut` becomes `DumpRequest` (worth having regardless — a debug-only dump shouldn't construct a transport). Module deployed at 24.9 MB, studio renders live through the stubbed client, no console errors.

**runewidth — replaced entirely in our code.** New `terminal/width.go` does the 0/1/2 classification from stdlib `unicode` categories plus `x/text/width`, both already linked, with a fast path for everything under U+0300 — which is nearly all of a prompt. Full suite passes including the 124-theme goldens, and the studio's `viewBox` is byte-identical, so no width drifted.

| | baseline | now |
|---|---|---|
| raw | 29,351,525 | 26,086,482 (**−11.1%**) |
| gzip | 6,640,090 | 5,945,286 (−10.5%) |
| brotli | 4,675,591 | 4,196,448 (**−10.2%**) |

**But "entirely" only holds for wasm.** The dep graph is clean there (0 references). The CLI still links runewidth through `cli/auth/tui` → bubbletea → `charmbracelet/x/ansi`, so it still pays 25 ms of init on every invocation. Removing that means not linking bubbletea, i.e. splitting the interactive commands into a separate binary — too big to do unasked.

I did prove the alternative: a lazy `sync.Once` around `initStrictWidthLUT` takes runewidth's init from 25 ms to 0.52 ms, and **total init across all 198 packages from 32.3 ms to 8.7 ms** — 23.6 ms off every prompt render. That needs an upstream PR or a published fork; I restored `go.mod`/`go.sum` rather than leave a `replace` pointing at `/tmp`. Your call on which route.

**The latent bug:** running the suite reverted `website/plugins/segments/registry.json`, putting `needsNerdFont` back. That file is *generated* by `src/config/segment_catalog_test.go`, and my earlier nerd-font commit removed the field from the JSON and the plugin but not from the generator — so any test run would have silently undone it, on anyone's machine. Fixed at the source: `segmentCatalogEntry` loses the field, and the `isNerdFontRune`/`needsNerdFont` helpers are gone.

`dsc` I left alone — I tried the cobra split expecting a clean no-build-tags win and it measured **−1,366 bytes**, i.e. noise. cobra wasn't the cost; the 37 KB is jsonschema and yaml/v4, reachable only via a tagged duplicate of a 134-line file. Bad trade for 0.9%, so I reverted it.

Not attempted: the empty-registry redesign. It's the larger win but it's the maps-fed-engine work, gated on segment detection no longer running in-browser — a feature, not a tweak.

perf(terminal): count cells without go-runewidth

Every length the writer computes is a sum of per-rune cell widths, and
go-runewidth answered that from its own Unicode tables. Since v0.0.27 it
also builds a 2.2MB lookup table in package init: 2.23 million calls
before main runs, measured at 25ms. oh-my-posh renders one prompt and
exits, so that was around 10% of a 240ms render, on every prompt, twice
per keystroke on shells that also draw a transient one.

The table is a cache, and a badly aimed one here. Measured over a
realistic 80-rune prompt it saved 48ns per render against the library's
own uncached path, so it needed something past half a million renders in
one process to pay for itself. It could not be turned off either:
Condition.RuneWidth only reads it when StrictEmojiNeutral is set, but
init builds it regardless.

runeCells answers the same question from the standard library's unicode
categories and golang.org/x/text/width, both already linked, with a fast
path for everything below U+0300 - which is nearly all of a prompt.

Checked against go-runewidth v0.0.27 across all 1,114,112 code points:
2,648 disagree, of which 2,048 are UTF-16 surrogates that cannot reach
this code, ~330 are wide symbol blocks no prompt contains (I Ching
hexagrams, Tai Xuan Jing, counting rods, Tangut) and ~150 are format and
tag characters where zero is the better answer. The real gap is ~70
recently assigned combining marks that x/text does not yet classify.
Every rune a prompt actually holds agrees exactly: emoji including flag
sequences, CJK, Nerd Font glyphs, powerline separators, box drawing,
accented Latin, common combining marks, Cyrillic and Greek.

The dependency stays in the module graph for now - bubbletea reaches it
through charmbracelet/x/ansi - so the CLI still pays that init until the
interactive commands stop being linked into the same binary. The wasm
build no longer references it at all.

Option 1 done, and the goldens carried the argument.

**Themes fixed** — `3fa916b0`. 18 segments across 11 themes now spell out the template they were already rendering, copied verbatim. The diff is **18 insertions, zero deletions**: line-level insertion, because re-stringifying the JSON would have reformatted 119 of the 124 themes and buried the change. `TestGoldenThemes` passes unchanged, which is the proof it's output-neutral — it pins rendered bytes for every bundled theme.

Two details worth recording. The insertion goes *before* the `"type"` line, never after: `type` is sometimes the object's last property with no trailing comma, and my first attempt appended after it and produced invalid JSON in all 11 files. And you were right to flag the escapes — `claude` (U+F0BC9), `nba` (U+F0806) and `ramadan` (U+1F319) carry astral glyphs written as Go's 8-digit `\U`, which isn't valid JSON and needs surrogate pairs in JS. I sidestepped hand-rolled unquoting entirely by dumping the defaults through Go's own `json.Marshal` and reading that back, so the pairs stay intact by construction.

**Table reverted.** The phase-1 commit is gone from history along with both files, and `defaultTemplate()` is dropped — the fallback is back to `segment.writer.Template()` guarded on the writer existing. So the engine is untouched: a config that omits a template still renders in a terminal exactly as before, and the contract you stated now holds for the shipped themes.

**Phase 2 landed** — `1e8b347b`. `templateContext()` returns the writer where one exists and the recorded data map where none does, and `restoreInto` picks the unmarshal destination to match. Behaviour is unchanged today because a writer is always constructed; it only removes the assumption that one must be.

Full suite green, both targets build, all four new commits verified individually, commitlint clean.

That leaves phases 3 and 4, and phase 1 disappearing has made them smaller:

- **Phase 3** — the recorder captures method results. Still needed: `.Working.String`, `.Status.String`, `.Premium.Percent.Gauge` and the rest of the 15 nested accesses are methods, and a map can't carry a method.
- **Phase 4** — tag the `Segments` map and the 117-entry `gob.Register` init behind `!(js && wasm)`.

The acceptance bar is unchanged: all 124 themes byte-identical through the CLI with segments and wasm without.

content.text:
Here's the situation in plain terms.

**The file is a pretend computer.** `segment_data.json` holds made-up facts — the user is `alice`, the folder is `~/dev/oh-my-posh`, the git branch is `main`. The studio renders from it so previews look like a real machine without being anyone's actual machine. Those names were chosen deliberately.

**The problem: some things aren't facts, they're answers.** The file says "2 files changed, 1 modified". But a git prompt doesn't print that — it prints a little summary like `+2 ~1`, which some code has to *work out* from the facts. Normally the browser has that code. We just deleted it, which is the whole point of the exercise: it was 4 MB.

So the answers now have to be written into the file ahead of time, next to the facts. That's what phase 3 taught the recorder to do.

**To write them, we run the real program once**, feed it the pretend facts, and let it write down both the facts and the answers it worked out. That part is settled. The only open question is how to make that one run cover all 117 segments.

**Path 1 — "go read every theme."** The recorder already has a mode that walks all 124 themes, collects every segment any of them mentions, and merges the lot into one file. It's exactly the coverage we want, and it exists.

The snag: that mode always switches on the privacy scrubber, because it was built for sharing fixtures publicly. The scrubber rubs out usernames, hostnames and paths and replaces them with generic ones. It would erase `alice` and `contoso-devbox` — the names we picked on purpose — and we'd get something anonymous instead.

The fix is small: tell the scrubber to leave alone any value that came from a hand-written file. Those values are already fake, so there's nothing to protect.

**Path 2 — "build one config with everything in it."** Instead of reading all the themes, we write a single config that mentions all 117 segments and record that one. No scrubber involved, so the chosen names survive untouched.

The snag: that config is a new thing to create and keep current. Add a segment next year and someone has to remember to add it there too, or it silently drops out of the studio.

**The difference that matters.** Path 1 reuses machinery that already stays in step with the themes automatically, and needs one small change to stop it scrubbing values we supplied. Path 2 avoids touching the scrubber but creates a list someone has to maintain by hand forever.

I'd take path 1. The scrubber change is honest on its own terms — it exists to protect real identity, and a value typed into a fixture by hand has none.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Weighs a subsystem by building the binary with its command registration removed, so the linker
# drops whatever only that command reached. Measures against a baseline built the same way.
#
# Registration removal, not file deletion: a command's Run closure is what makes its transitive
# dependencies reachable, and dropping the AddCommand call is what lets the linker prove nothing
# else needs them.
set -u
cd /d/oh-my-posh/src || exit 1

SCRATCH="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/weigh"
rm -rf "$SCRATCH" && mkdir -p "$SCRATCH"

build() {
  local label="$1" overlay="$2"
  local out="$SCRATCH/$label.exe"
  if [ -n "$overlay" ]; then
    go build -ldflags "-s -w" -overlay "$overlay" -o "$out" . 2>"$SCRATCH/$label.err"
  else
    go build -ldflags "-s -w" -o "$out" . 2>"$SCRATCH/$label.err"
  fi
  if [ ! -f "$out" ]; then
    echo "BUILD FAILED: $label"; head -3 "$SCRATCH/$label.err"; return 1
  fi
  stat -c%s "$out"
}

# Rewrites one file with the given sed program, returning an overlay JSON pointing at the copy.
overlay_for() {
  local name="$1"; shift
  local json="$SCRATCH/$name.json"
  local replacements=""
  for spec in "$@"; do
    local file="${spec%%::*}"
    local prog="${spec#*::}"
    local copy="$SCRATCH/$name-$(echo "$file" | tr '/' '_')"
    sed "$prog" "$file" > "$copy"
    [ -n "$replacements" ] && replacements="$replacements,"
    replacements="$replacements\"$PWD/$file\":\"$copy\""
  done
  printf '{"Replace":{%s}}' "$replacements" > "$json"
  echo "$json"
}

BASE=$(build baseline "") || exit 1
echo "baseline: $BASE bytes"
echo

report() {
  local label="$1" size="$2"
  awk -v b="$BASE" -v s="$size" -v l="$label" \
    'BEGIN{printf "%-26s %11d   -%9d  (-%.2f%%)\n", l, s, b-s, (b-s)/b*100}'
}

I have to correct my own measurement before answering: **the first attempt was invalid.** Removing `AddCommand` registrations gave −0.00% for all four subsystems, because cobra commands are package-level vars — their `Run` closures stay reachable whether or not they're registered. That proved nothing.

**On the recorder specifically: I don't have a valid number yet.** What I can say is `config_export_data.go` (348 lines) + `sanitize.go` (235) + `segment_data.go` (151) is ~734 lines, and its dependencies — `encoding/json`, `reflect`, `os` — are already linked for other reasons, so the marginal cost is probably small. But "probably" isn't a number and I won't hand you one dressed as one.

You're right that it's odd on principle, though. `config export data --themes --sanitize` exists **solely to generate mock fixtures**. Nothing a user does at a prompt touches it.

**The inventory of what ships but doesn't render prompts:**

| Subsystem | Size | Purpose | Notable dependency |
|---|---|---|---|
| `config export data` + sanitize | ~734 lines | generating fixtures | — |
| `src/svg` + image/svg export | ~1,300 lines | docs, sharing | — |
| `cli/font` (+TUI) | 835 lines | font installer | bubbletea |
| `cli/upgrade` (+TUI) | 562 lines | self-update | bubbletea |
| `cli/auth` (+TUI) | 409 lines | OAuth flows | **bubbletea** |
| `src/dsc` | 186 lines | desired-state config | **jsonschema**, cobra |
| `cli/serve` | 345 lines | daemon mode | — |
| `claude`, `copilot` | ~70 lines | integrations | — |

Genuinely core to rendering: `print`, `init`, `shell`, `stream`, `statusline`, and config loading.

**The interesting one is bubbletea**, because it costs more than bytes. `go mod why` traces it to `cli/auth/tui`, and it's what drags in `go-runewidth` — the 25 ms of `init` on *every* prompt render we measured earlier. I stubbed the auth and upgrade TUIs to price it: **−53,760 bytes (0.31%)**, but runewidth's init survived, and tracing showed `charmbracelet/x/ansi`, `x/cellbuf`, `muesli/ansi` and `bubbles/textinput` still linked through `cli/font/tui`, which I hadn't stubbed. So that 53 KB is a partial figure, not the TUI cost.

Two caveats worth stating plainly. The startup numbers are noisy on this machine — the same binary read 32.3 ms and 92.8 ms of total init across two runs, so the 25 ms runewidth figure is reproducible but the totals around it need repeated sampling. And a proper per-subsystem size answer needs stub overlays for each package, not registration removal.

The question underneath yours is the real one: **should a prompt engine that runs twice per keystroke also contain a font installer, an OAuth browser flow, a self-updater and an SVG renderer?** Splitting the interactive commands into a second binary would drop bubbletea and its 25 ms entirely from the hot path — that's ~10% of a 240 ms render, and it's the single biggest latency item found today.

I can build the stub harness properly and give you a real per-subsystem table — roughly one overlay per package. Worth doing before any decision about splitting, and I'd rather do that than guess. Want it?

input.description: Analyse replacing bubbletea
input.prompt:
Analyse whether oh-my-posh can drop the bubbletea TUI framework entirely and replace it with a small purpose-built terminal UI. Produce a design proposal backed by measurement. This is analysis and measurement only — do NOT change committed source. Any experiment must be reverted, and you must never run `git stash` (the main session has uncommitted work).

Write findings to `D:\oh-my-posh\.bubbletea-analysis.md` as you go, appending after each finding. Two previous background agents died when the parent process exited and lost everything held in memory — that file is your deliverable, so keep it current rather than saving everything for a final answer.

## Why this is being asked

oh-my-posh is a prompt engine. It runs once or twice per keystroke, as a short-lived process, and startup latency is the product. Measured on this machine: a full prompt render is ~240ms, and `go-runewidth`'s package init alone is 25ms of it — roughly 10%. That init exists only because bubbletea's dependency `charmbracelet/x/ansi` pulls go-runewidth in, and Go runs every linked package's init before main regardless of which subcommand the user invoked. A user typing at a prompt pays for a font-installer UI they are not using.

content.text:
Measured before disrupting anything, and the number changes the picture: **the SVG renderer costs the CLI 37,376 bytes — 0.22%** of a 17.3 MB binary.

For that 0.22%, moving it to wasm-only costs:

- **`oh-my-posh config export image` disappears.** It's a documented user command with a full section in [data.mdx](website/docs/configuration/data.mdx), and this branch *just* changed it — `feat(cli)!: export a config to SVG instead of PNG` is commit `3dc450b2`. Users would go from "your PNG export is now SVG" to "there is no image export" in one release.
- **Both website generators break.** [export_themes.mjs:205](website/export_themes.mjs:205) and [render-segment-previews.mjs:70](website/scripts/render-segment-previews.mjs:70) shell out to that command for the 124-theme gallery and 117 segment previews. They'd need rewriting to instantiate `omp.wasm` from Node — feasible, and it would drop 241 process spawns from the build, but it's a real piece of work, not a side effect.

So it's a breaking change plus a pipeline rewrite, for less than a quarter of one percent.

The rest of the picture, for comparison: `src/svg` is 1,154 lines but imported by exactly one file (`render/render.go`), so it's already well isolated — a `js && wasm` tag on it is mechanically easy. The reason it's cheap in bytes is that it's pure string assembly over `terminal.Run`; it pulls no dependencies of its own. It isn't what's making the binary big.

By contrast the thing that *is* expensive sits in the TUIs — 25 ms of `go-runewidth` init on every prompt render, which is ~10% of a 240 ms render. That's what Fable is analysing now.

I've held off executing, because I don't think you'd choose this trade knowing it's 0.22% against losing the command. Three ways forward:

1. **Leave it.** 37 KB isn't worth a breaking change; revisit if the CLI ever needs to shrink for real.
2. **Do it anyway**, and migrate the two generators to a Node+wasm renderer first so the docs build keeps working. The command still goes away for users.
3. **Tag it wasm-only but keep the CLI command**, which is contradictory — the command needs the encoder — so this isn't actually available.

Say which and I'll go. The scratch stubs are cleaned up; the working tree still holds the seven uncommitted files from phases 3 and 4.

content.text:
Bubbletea analysis is in, and the contrast with the SVG question is stark.

**The cost is much bigger than my partial 53 KB suggested.** Stubbing all four charm consumers — it found a fourth I'd missed, `cli/progress`, alongside the three TUI packages:

| | with | without |
|---|---|---|
| binary | 24,398,336 | 22,560,256 (**−1.84 MB, −7.5%**) |
| init, median of 15 runs | 39.3 ms | **6.95 ms** (−83%) |
| `print primary`, median of 21 runs | 141.8 ms | **97.7 ms** (−31% per prompt) |

Sixteen modules leave the build entirely — go-runewidth, all eight charmbracelet modules, muesli, `atotto/clipboard` (the one this repo already carries a fork of). That last one is worth noting: the fork exists to patch a dependency that would leave with bubbletea.

**And the capability being paid for is almost nothing.** The entire interactive surface is one non-filtering select list (the font picker), spinners, progress bars, and quit keys. No text input, no alternate screen, no mouse. `font install --headless` already exists, and the upgrade UI's logic is already callback-decoupled through `report.go`.

The insight that makes a replacement small: **raw mode is only needed for arrow-key selection.** Spinners and progress bars are `\r`-repaint output that works fine in cooked mode. So a numbered-list picker needs no terminal-state handling at all — no termios, no Windows console modes, no restore-on-panic. That's ~250–300 lines with zero new dependencies, or ~400–480 if you want arrow keys via `golang.org/x/term` (not currently linked, though its only dependency `x/sys` already is). Net: roughly 1,080 lines deleted for ~300 added.

It rejected both alternatives with reasons: every lighter TUI library it checked pulls go-runewidth — the exact cost being removed — and the second-binary split saves the same 40 ms while adding packaging, self-upgrade and version-skew problems across every distribution channel.

**Put beside the SVG move: 0.22% and a breaking change, versus 7.5% and 31% off every prompt render.** Your instinct that a small purpose-built engine could replace it looks right, and it's a far better use of the effort. I'd park the SVG move and do this instead.

Two housekeeping notes. The full analysis is in `.bubbletea-analysis.md` (15 KB, untracked) — I'll bin it once you've read it. And Fable deleted `src/terminal/terminal.test.exe`, a gitignored compiled-test leftover that predated this session; regenerable with `go test -c`, but it flagged the deletion itself rather than staying quiet about it, which was the right call.

Still open and unchanged: the SVG decision, and the seven uncommitted files from phases 3 and 4 — including the fixture question about how `segment_data.json` gets its method results reproducibly.

feat(cli): record what a segment's methods return

A recorded data file held a writer's fields. Templates read more than
fields: `{{ .Working.Added }}` reads one and `{{ .Working.String }}`
calls a method, and a template neither knows nor cares which. Replayed
against the writer struct that difference stays invisible, because the
methods come back with it. Replayed against the data alone it does not -
nothing can carry a method - so a template calling one found nothing
where a terminal found a string.

The recorder now walks the writer's exported zero-argument methods and
records what they returned, two levels deep, recovering from any that
panic. Go resolves a name against a map key exactly as it resolves it
against a method, so the recorded result reads identically.

--data joins the command for the same reason the image and print
commands carry it, plus one: a fixture recorded once can be re-recorded
through the writers to pick up whatever the format has since gained,
without giving up the values it was curated with.
EOF

content.content:
### 2. What the TUIs actually do (capability inventory)

The task brief was slightly stale. The real consumer set is four packages, and prior
decoupling work has already pushed all business logic out of two of them:

**`src/cli/progress` (65 lines, model.go + reader.go)** — shared wrapper.
- `bubbles/progress` bar with a scaled purple-pink gradient (model.go:12).
- `Reader` that wraps an `io.Reader` and `program.Send()`s percent messages (reader.go:25).
- `Model.View()` appends `terminal.SetProgress()` — the ConEmu/Windows Terminal OSC 9;4
  taskbar-progress escape, which is oh-my-posh's own code, not charm's (model.go:28).
- Imported by `cli/font` (tui.go, download.go) and `cli/upgrade/tui`.

**`src/cli/auth/tui` (tui.go 115, copilot.go 216, ytmda.go 150 lines)** — display-only shell.
- One spinner (`bubbles/spinner`, Globe) + static text lines (tui.go:60-103).
- `lipgloss.NewStyle().Margin(1,0,2,2)` and one foreground colour (tui.go:26, :63).
- NO key handling, NO list, NO text input, NO resize handling, NO alternate screen,
  NO mouse. The user never types anything; ctrl+c works only via bubbletea's built-in
  interrupt. The device-code OAuth flows (HTTP polling loops) run in plain goroutines
  (copilot.go:81-117, ytmda.go:44-75) and poke the UI via `program.Send(stateMsg)`.
- The UI is literally: spinner + "Please visit URL and enter code XYZ" + final status line.

**`src/cli/upgrade/tui` (167 lines)** — display-only shell.
- Spinner (Dot/Moon/Jump variants per stage), progress bar, `q`/`esc`/`ctrl+c` to quit
  (tui.go:79-85), lipgloss margin. No list, no input, no resize, no altscreen, no mouse.
- The upgrade itself is ALREADY fully decoupled: `cli/upgrade` exposes
  `SetStageReporter`/`SetProgressReporter` plain callbacks (report.go:31, :50), added
  precisely so the core never imports bubbletea (its package comment says the import
  graph must compile for wasm, where bubbletea does not build). The TUI is a subscriber.

**`src/cli/font` tui.go (367 lines; not a subpackage)** — the only real interaction.
- `bubbles/list` with a custom delegate — but with filtering DISABLED and status bar off
  (tui.go:94-95), and up/down/j/k selection overridden by hand for wrap-around
  (tui.go:230-248). So of the list widget it uses: render N rows + highlight one +
  pagination. The fuzzy-filter/textinput machinery of `bubbles/list` is linked but unused
  (`go list -deps bubbles/list` pulls `textinput`, `sahilm/fuzzy`, `go-runewidth`).
- Keys handled: up/down/j/k, enter, q/esc/ctrl+c (tui.go:201-249).
- Spinner (Dot/Globe), progress bar, `tea.WindowSizeMsg` → `list.SetWidth` (tui.go:194).
- A headless path ALREADY EXISTS: `font.Run(font, zipFolder, headless)` →
  `installHeadless()` (tui.go:331-337, :353-366), used by `font install --zip-folder ... <name>`
  when headless is set. Download/unzip/install logic lives in download.go/install.go,
  UI-free except for `progress.NewReader(..., program)` at download.go:85.

**Summary: across the whole binary the interactive surface is one non-filtering
select-list (font picker), spinners, progress bars, and quit keys.** No text input, no
alternate screen, no mouse, no filtering. Auth and upgrade UIs are pure spinner/status
displays over already-callback-decoupled business logic.

One structural note for later: unlike upgrade (whose install logic is charm-free in
`cli/upgrade` with reporter callbacks), the auth device-code HTTP flows live INSIDE the
tea models (`cli/auth/tui/copilot.go`, `ytmda.go`). Dropping bubbletea means moving
~300 lines of already-working HTTP logic into plain functions with a status callback —
a mechanical extraction following the pattern `cli/upgrade/report.go` already set.

### 3. What a purpose-built replacement needs

The key observation that shrinks this from "framework" to "small utility": **raw mode is
only needed for the arrow-key list.** Spinners, progress bars, and status updates are
pure output — `\r` + erase-line (`ESC[2K`) repainting works fine in cooked mode, which
is how the auth and upgrade UIs can be rebuilt with zero terminal-state risk. Only the
font picker reads keys.

Pieces, with LOC estimates (calibrated against the existing code sizes):

| Piece | LOC | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Status-line renderer (spinner + message, `\r`/`ESC[2K` repaint, hide/show cursor) | ~80 | ticker goroutine + `Set(msg)`; cooked mode; `src/terminal` already owns ANSI writing |
| Progress bar renderer | ~50 | percent → filled bar; `terminal.SetProgress` (OSC 9;4) already exists at `src/terminal/features.go`; drop the purple-pink lipgloss gradient or reuse the repo's own gradient writer |
| Select list (highlight, wrap-around, 14-row page) | ~120 | replicates exactly what tui.go:84-100,230-248 uses of `bubbles/list` |

content.content:
| Select list (highlight, wrap-around, 14-row page) | ~120 | replicates exactly what tui.go:84-100,230-248 uses of `bubbles/list` |
| Raw mode enter/restore | ~40 with `golang.org/x/term`, ~120 hand-rolled | see hazards below |
| Key decoder (arrows CSI `A`/`B`, enter, esc, `q`, `j`/`k`, ctrl+c) | ~80 | tiny state machine; bare-ESC disambiguation via short read deadline |
| Cleanup on panic/interrupt (restore mode, show cursor) | ~30 | `defer` + `os/signal` |
| **Total** | **~400 (with x/term) / ~480 (without)** | one new `src/cli/ui` package |

For scale: the code being deleted is ~1,080 lines (font tui.go 367, auth/tui 481,
upgrade/tui 167, cli/progress 65), of which ~300 (auth HTTP flows) move rather than
vanish. The replacement is smaller than what it removes.

Cross-platform hazards, concretely:
- **Windows console**: raw input needs `SetConsoleMode` with
  `ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT` so arrows arrive as CSI sequences; output side needs
  `ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING` (oh-my-posh's init path already assumes VT output
  works — the whole prompt is ANSI). `golang.org/x/term.MakeRaw` handles both console
  modes on Windows and termios on POSIX in one call.
- **`golang.org/x/term` availability**: in the module graph today only via gookit test
  packages — NOT linked into the binary (verified: absent from stub buildinfo, and
  `go.mod` has no require). Adding it as a direct require costs one tiny module whose
  only dependency is `golang.org/x/sys`, which is already a direct dependency and
  already linked. No init tables, no measurable init cost. [Not measured, but the
  package is two files of syscall wrappers.]
- **MSYS/mintty/Cygwin ptys**: stdin is a pipe, not a console; `MakeRaw` fails. Handle
  by falling back to the numbered-list cooked-mode picker (or headless) when
  `term.IsTerminal(stdin)` is false — the repo has form here: `--headless` already
  exists on `font install` (cli/font.go:95).
- **Resize**: currently used only for `list.SetWidth` (tui.go:194). Render
  width-independent lines and drop resize handling entirely; SIGWINCH does not exist on
  Windows and bubbletea itself polls there. Zero user-visible loss for a 14-row list of
  short font names.
- **Restore on panic**: one `defer restore()` in the single entry point plus a
  SIGINT/SIGTERM handler; bubbletea's value here is real but replicable in ~30 lines
  because there is exactly one raw-mode call site.

### 4. Alternatives to writing one

**(a) A lighter third-party library.** [Assessed from dependency knowledge, not built
and measured.] Every mainstream Go prompt/TUI library — promptui, survey (archived),
pterm, huh — pulls `go-runewidth` (or the whole charm stack) for cell-width alignment,
which is precisely the 27-33ms init we are trying to shed. Any library linked into the
main binary pays its init on every prompt render regardless of subcommand. Given the
needed surface is ~400 lines, a third-party dependency buys nothing and risks
re-importing the same tables. Not recommended.

**(b) Non-interactive / cooked-mode variants.** The only true interaction is the font
picker. A numbered list (`print 1..N, read a line`) needs no raw mode, no key decoder,
=== recommendation ===
## Ranked recommendation

Measured stake, from (1): **−44ms median on every prompt render (−31%), −32ms of init
(−83%), −1.8MB binary (−7.5%), 16 modules dropped.** This clears any reasonable bar for
acting.

1. **Do: replace bubbletea with a small in-repo `cli/ui` package, cooked-mode-first**
   (options b+c+d above): status-line spinner, `\r`-repainted progress bar, numbered
   font picker; auth HTTP flows extracted to plain functions with status callbacks.
   ~250-300 new lines, ~1,080 deleted, zero new dependencies, no raw-mode risk.
   User-visible change: font picker becomes number+Enter; upgrade loses its `q`-to-quit
   key. Effort: roughly a day including tests; the hard part (decoupled business
   logic) already exists for upgrade and is a mechanical move for auth.
2. **Optional polish on top of 1: arrow-key font picker via `golang.org/x/term`**
   (+~150 lines: MakeRaw, key decoder, restore-on-panic; cooked fallback when stdin is
   not a terminal). Preserves today's exact interaction. Take it only if number+Enter
   feels like a regression in review — the risk (terminal state corruption on the long
   tail of Windows consoles and MSYS ptys) is the only real risk in this whole plan.
3. **Don't: adopt a lighter TUI library** — the viable ones link go-runewidth, which is
   the single largest init cost being removed. [Assessed, not measured.]
4. **Don't: split a second binary** — same measured win as option 1 but with packaging,
   self-upgrade, and version-skew costs across every distribution channel.

Cleanup note: all experiment artifacts (stubs, overlay.json, test binaries) live in the
session scratchpad; `git status` of the repo is untouched by this analysis.

number and Enter needs none of that, and works when stdin is redirected,

content.text:
Committed, and bubbletea is underway.

**Three commits landed first**, as asked — the `--data` themes hook folded into the recorder commit it belongs to, and the wasm groundwork separately:

```
22efa3f2 feat(cli): add a terminal UI that a prompt engine can afford
ff344fae feat(website): render the site's artifacts without spawning the CLI
7faafac4 feat(config): leave the segment implementations out of the browser build
5db4dbd4 feat(cli): record what a segment's methods return
```

**The `cli/ui` package is in** — 81% covered, suite green, nothing using it yet so nothing can break.

Fable's analysis reshaped what I built. The framework is doing far less than its weight suggests: across the entire binary the interactive surface is **one non-filtering select list, spinners, progress bars and quit keys**. No text input, no alternate screen, no mouse. And two of the four consumers are already display-only shells over callback-decoupled logic — `cli/upgrade` exposes `SetStageReporter`/`SetProgressReporter` precisely so the core never imports bubbletea.

The observation that shrank this from "framework" to "utility": **raw mode is only needed for arrow keys.** Spinners and progress bars are a carriage return and an erase-line away from repainting themselves. So everything writes in cooked mode — no termios, no Windows console modes, nothing to restore if the process panics. That's the class of bug that leaves a terminal unusable after a crash, and this design simply doesn't have it.

The picker is numbered rather than arrow-driven for the same reason, with a side benefit: it works when stdin is redirected, which is how anyone scripts an install. Tests cover the ends that bite — an overshooting `content-length` driving the bar past 100% would panic on a negative repeat count, and `Stop` on a never-started status must not panic on a nil channel, since a deferred `Stop` runs even when the path that would have started it returned early.

**What's left is the migration**, four packages in increasing order of difficulty:

1. `cli/progress` (65 lines) — the shared wrapper, straight swap.
2. `cli/upgrade/tui` (167) — display-only, logic already decoupled.
3. `cli/auth/tui` (481) — the real work: ~300 lines of device-code OAuth polling live *inside* the tea models and need extracting to plain functions with a status callback, following the pattern `cli/upgrade/report.go` already set.
4. `cli/font` tui.go (367) — the picker.

Then dropping bubbletea, lipgloss, bubbles and 13 other modules from `go.mod`, and re-measuring against Fable's baseline: **−1.84 MB, −44 ms per render, −83% init**.

One user-visible change to flag now rather than at the end: the font picker becomes number-and-Enter, and the upgrade UI loses its `q`-to-quit. Fable's optional step 2 restores arrow keys via `golang.org/x/term` for ~150 lines, but that reintroduces the only real risk in the plan, so I'd leave it out unless the numbered picker feels like a regression when you see it.

content.text:
Bubbletea is gone. The reframe made it much simpler than reimplementing the picker — a CLI already has a way to answer "which fonts are there".

```
oh-my-posh font list          # one name per line, greppable, pipeable
oh-my-posh font install Meslo
```

**Measured on the real binary:**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| binary | 17,330,176 | 15,981,056 (**−7.8%**) |
| init, median of 11 runs | 39.3 ms | **6.8 ms** |

That init cost was paid on *every* invocation, prompt renders included. `go-runewidth`'s 2.2 MB lookup table — the one nothing in the prompt path ever read — is gone with it.

**20 modules left**, and one of them is worth noting: `atotto/clipboard`, which this repo carries a *patched fork* of via a `replace` directive. Bubbletea was the only thing that needed it, so the fork and the directive both went. `go.mod` now has zero replace directives.

The whole migration came to four packages:

- `cli/upgrade/tui` — logic was already callback-decoupled, so it just needed a different subscriber.
- `cli/auth/tui` — device-code polling moved out of the tea models; `Run` drives it synchronously now, since the status line redraws from its own ticker.
- `cli/font` — the TUI deleted outright, replaced by two subcommands over primitives that were already UI-free (`fonts()`, `ResolveFontAsset`, `Download`, `InstallZIP`).
- `cli/progress` — deleted; its byte-counting reader moved into `cli/ui` taking a callback instead of a program.

Two breaking changes, both in the commit footer: `font install` now requires a name, and `--headless` is gone since it existed only to skip the picker.
